LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & EVERYDAY OBJECTS · AGES 6–9 MONTHS

Dog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Dogs perform themselves: the sound is famous, the wag is famous, and the baby version of both is arriving right about now. This lesson stages the dog card as a two-part act.

What is this?

A dog is a four-legged friend that barks, wags and adores outings — and it is the animal your baby is likeliest to meet in the flesh. The card gives a clear portrait; your woof and your floppy-ear hands give it a performance your baby can join.

What does it mean?

Two channels are better than one: a word with a sound and an action offers your baby two roads in. Some babies answer sounds first, some answer movement, and a few manage both — whichever road your baby takes, the word waits at the end of it.

What does the child need to know?

The act is simple: the woof, then the ear-flap hands, then silence. And across the week, say the word about every dog there is — enormous, tiny, loud, asleep — because at this stage your baby is learning that one name covers a whole population of very different animals.

Why this matters

Dog is often the first animal word a child owns outright, because dogs supply so many rehearsals: on walks, in books, behind fences, on the telly. Owning the word turns every future dog into a named event — and named events are how a baby’s world gets organised.

What it teaches

Sound recognition and imitation, action imitation (the copy-me wave of the next stage starts here), generalisation across different-looking examples, and reaction-and-recovery to sudden noises.

Words to learn

dogwoofwagearsbigsmall

Say this to your child

““Dog! A great big happy dog, tongue out, tail going. A dog says woof! Woof, woof! And look — my hands are floppy ears. Big dogs say woof, small dogs say woof, sleepy dogs say woof. Everyone knows this word by heart.””

Step by step

  1. Bring the card to viewing distance and greet it: “Dog! Look at that happy face.”
  2. Tap the tail and give it a wiggle with your fingertip — the wag is the dog’s signature, and yours to perform.
  3. Do the woof — two short friendly ones — then pat your own head like floppy ears while your baby watches.
  4. Hold the silence open. A laugh, a kick, a babble that sounds like a reply: answer all of it with delight.
  5. Across the week, replay the word at every dog you meet — the giant one, the yappy one, the sleeping one — same word, every size.

Look closer at the picture

The artwork is a happy dog with its tongue out and tail mid-wag — say that much. The live noticing: which part of the act does your baby copy — the sound, the hand-movement, or neither yet? Imitation at this stage is a coin with two faces, and either face counts.

Ask your child

Watch the copying: does a hand wave after your ear-flaps? Does a sound follow your woof? Wonder aloud: “I wonder which of us is training which — you have me doing this dog three times a day.”

What your child can say or do

A babbled burst right after the woof, arms that flap when yours do, a full-leg jiggle of joy, or a solemn stare that saves its reaction for the third round — copy-me behaviour at 6–9 months rarely fires on the first performance, so keep the act in rotation.

Out in the real world

Dogs are everywhere once you start counting: the neighbour’s behind the gate, the one asleep outside the café, every other page of the animal book. Each is a replay of word, sound and — if your hands are free — ears.

Try it together

Woof-and-freeze: do the woof, then go completely still with an expectant face. The stillness is the invitation; whatever noise or movement your baby loads into it, celebrate like it was a word. Because functionally, it was.

Understanding check

Parent self-check: did the word cover more than one dog this week, and did the act get a silence at the end for your baby’s half? The variety teaches the generalisation; the silence teaches the conversation.

Parent tips

Commit to the performance — an apologetic woof teaches half a word. If your baby startles hard at the sound, drop the volume and keep the ears; some babies take the visual road first and find the sound later. Both roads are open.

Staying safe

Real dogs are met only on their owner’s terms and at a safe distance — the card carries the lesson and the fence carries the dog. Watch reaction-and-recovery: a startle that settles fast is healthy; a baby who cannot settle needs the quiet version of this card.
